closeout.claim: On the evening of Jun 30 A. P. Hill reached Cashtown. He was told of Pettigrew's reconnaissance toward Gettysburg: enemy cavalry near the town. The three accounts differ on what Pettigrew reported (principally cavalry, force not determined; a large force of cavalry supported by infantry; cavalry, with drums heard beyond the town). Hill judged the only force at Gettysburg to be cavalry, probably a detachment of observation (Heth, 1877), and intended to advance next morning to find out what was in his front.

closeout.claim: Lee decided to concentrate the army east of the mountains; Hill's corps was ordered toward Cashtown on the 29th and Ewell, recalled from Carlisle, was directed to join the army at Cashtown or Gettysburg as circumstances might require. Ewell received that order at Heidlersburg on the night of Jun 30, with a note from Hill saying he was at Cashtown; Early was told the object was to concentrate the corps at or near Cashtown. The row's "Lee orders concentration around Cashtown, Jun 30 evening" is a receipt time at Heidlersburg, not the hour Lee issued the order.
remains_unsupported: Hour of issue and text of Lee's order (not in the reports; Lee's own report gives dates only).

Campfires, cooking, civilians in the camps and the state of the sky that night are not documented; one recollection has the stars out and the moon up.

library_passages.verbatim: The opening gun of the battle was fired by the Confederates, the shot coming from a cannon in Marye's Virginia Battery, posted on the Chambersburg Pike on the first ridge west of Willoughby Run. Calef's Horse Battery — A, Second United States Artillery— which was attached to Buford's Division, replied promptly from its position near the Chambersburg Pike, and the battle of Gettysburg began.

closeout.claim: Heth: on reaching the second ridge west of Gettysburg a few shots from Pegram's battalion (Marye's battery) scattered the cavalry vedettes; Archer's brigade then stood in line on the right of the pike and Davis's on the left, and both were directed to advance as a forced reconnaissance. Neither Heth nor Hill says the guns failed to move the cavalry. Beveridge instead has Archer cross the Marsh Creek bridge and deploy skirmishers on the right of the pike, then Davis north of it. The two sequences and their hours are carried as scenarios.
remains_unsupported: The row's claim that the guns failed; the hour of the deployment.

closeout.claim: In a letter of 18 October 1865 to Maj. Gen. Hancock (the original is in the Bachelder Papers; it is printed in a 1989 U.S. Army War College study, which was read, the original was not seen) the signal officer Aaron B. Jerome says that he was sent back to find a prominent position and watch the enemy; that as early as seven A.M. he reported their advance and took his station in the steeple of the "Theological Seminary"; that Buford came up and looked at them through his glass and then formed his small cavalry force; that, looking toward Emmitsburg, he called Buford's attention to an army corps advancing about two miles off and distinguished it as the "first" by its "corps flag"; and that Buford held on, unaided, for half an hour against a whole corps of the rebels until Reynolds and a few of his staff rode up at a gallop and hailed Buford, who was with him in the steeple. The New York commission history (1900) and Bachelder (1873) tell the same scene without his name. No report of 1863 states it, and Weld's diary of 1863 has Reynolds talk with Buford in a field on the right of the road (T1-096): both are carried as scenarios. Jerome gives "seven A.M." and "half an hour" and no clock time for the meeting.
remains_unsupported: The ladder from the attic to the cupola; a clock time for the sighting and for Reynolds' arrival at the steeple (Jerome gives "seven A.M." and "half an hour"); Jerome's letter was read only as printed in a 1989 study, the original (Bachelder Papers, U.S. Army Military History Institute) was not seen.

closeout.claim: The observer was Jerome himself: in his letter of 18 October 1865 (read as printed in a 1989 U.S. Army War College study; original not seen) he says that, looking toward Emmitsburg from the steeple of the Theological Seminary, he called Buford's attention to an army corps advancing some two miles off and distinguished it as the First by its corps flag; Buford held on for half an hour, unaided, until Reynolds rode up. The New York commission history (1900) has the signal officer in the belfry see the First Corps flag on the Emmitsburg road after the fight had raged for over an hour, without naming him. That Jerome served with Buford at Gettysburg is documented (Buford; Brown 1896 roster). No source gives a clock time for the sighting; if Reynolds met Buford at about ten (Weld via Meade 1913) the sighting was about half an hour earlier, about 09:30 (inferred).
remains_unsupported: A clock time for the sighting (the row's about 10:00 is not stated by any source; about 09:30 is inferred from two relative statements).

closeout.claim: Reynolds fell as the attack began: about 10.15 a.m. (Doubleday, Wadsworth), about 10 (Beveridge 1891), 11.15 (Howard's 5 p.m. dispatch) with the news reaching Howard about 11.30. Weld: struck in the back of the neck by a volley while placing the Wisconsin brigade, killed almost instantly; Bachelder: killed in the grove, shot through the head at almost the first volley; Indiana (1913): at the first volley of Archer's brigade; Heth: one of the first shells fired by Pegram mortally wounded him. Bates (1875): as the leading regiment (the 2nd Wisconsin) approached the wood Reynolds joined the charge, turned to look for his supports and was struck in the brain, the woods being full of sharp-shooters; the New York commission narrative (1900) has him leading forward the 19th Indiana when he fell, about 10:15. The default under the recorded delegated decision C-040 is the window 10:15 to 11:15; the PDF's 10:30 and 10:40-10:50 stay selectable. The row's "show a rifle round, not a shell" is one scenario; Heth's shell is another.
remains_unsupported: East or west of the McPherson Ridge crest (the grove itself and both regiment claims are documented).

closeout.claim: Howard went to the top of a high building in Gettysburg, the observatory on Fahnestock's store (Biddle), saw the fighting near the railroad cut, and, about 11.30 by his watch, heard of Reynolds' death; he judged the only tenable position for his limited force to be the ridge southeast of the town and set his headquarters near the cemetery. Schurz joined him before 12 m. and received his instructions for the Eleventh Corps; about 12.30 (Howard) the head of the Eleventh Corps entered and passed through the town, and Pierce (1914) has Schurz's division entering Gettysburg at 12:45, so the row's window ending at 12:00 is earlier than both.

closeout.claim: Norton (signal officer): a station of observation was established on Jul 1, first on the college and then on the court-house. Jacobs (1864): at about 8:30 a.m. one of the General's (Howard's) signal officers was on the College cupola making observations and was directed by a College officer to Cemetery Hill; Howard's own report has him on a high building in the town only shortly before the news of Reynolds' death at about 11.30 a.m. (OR p.701-702), so the 8:30 hour is Jacobs's claim and no source confirms an observer of Howard's party at that hour. Battles and Leaders: the cupola was first used by Union officers and then by Confederate as a station for observation and signals. A 1989 U.S. Army War College study names the building: the cupola of Pennsylvania Hall at Gettysburg College (a plaque on the hall marks a Union signal station), where Jerome's station was moved from the Lutheran Seminary cupola, and on 1 July to the courthouse; the study names no source for those dates. Jacobs's own presence with Union officers in the cupola and the Confederate use on the evening of Jul 1 are not stated by any source read.
remains_unsupported: Prof. Jacobs in the cupola; the hour at which the cupola passed to the Confederates (Jacobs: Lee used it on Jul 2); a source for the dates of Jerome's changes of station.
